newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Oil price rally triggered by barge accident.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil price rally triggered by barge accident.

text.p: Crude oil prices rallied sharply in New York Tuesday amid talk that a barge accident in the Mississippi River would disrupt oil shipments, triggering a feverish round of short covering.

"The talk du jour is the Mississippi River. There is a good amount (of refined product) that is shipped, but I think the story is a bit overblown," said Thomas Blakeslee, analyst with Cargill Investor Services in New York.
Crude for April delivery on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) settled up $1.14 at $22.06 a barrel.
April heating oil finished up 1.88 cents a gallon at 56.18 cents while April gasoline ended up 2.22 cents a gallon at 67.48 cents.
The Mississippi River remains closed indefinitely as workers clean up after a string of 25 barges hit a bridge in north Baton Rouge, Lousiana late Monday, the Coast Guard said Tuesday.

The river was already swollen due to flooding in its northern part. An unknown quantity of petro-chemical product has leaked, and local officials ordered a precautionary evacuation of residents and businesses in the vicinity, authorities said.
"There was a lot of short covering by paper (futures)," said Al Lindseth, manager of oil and gas hedge programs with GSC Energy in Atlanta, noting large funds bought crude and refined products.
But, traders said crude and gasoline in particular have been oversold after consolidating for more than a month amid a seasonal decline in oil prices.

"The gasoline market was polishing itself for a rally for quite some time. The Mississippi River story has little to do with it," said John Bradberry, vice president at Transmontaigne Products Services Inc in Fayettville, Ark.

Bradberry said only about 10 to 15 percent of refined product used north of Baton Rouge is received by the Mississippi River. Instead, he said gasoline is starting its traditional spring rally which occurs in anticipation of the summer driving season when gasoline demand peaks.
The short covering eclipsed anticipation of this evening's weekly inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API).

After the market's close, the API said for the week ended March 14, crude stocks rose a mere 76,000 barrels while distillate stocks dropped 3.54 million barrels and gasoline stocks dropped 4.32 million barrels.
Refined product stocks declined much more than anticipated while crude stocks grew much less, a typically bullish scenario for oil prices.
